docs.title: The Ops Garage
docs.text:
Welcome to The Ops Garage — my public technical notebook for cyber operations, home lab infrastructure, automation, GRC, and project work.

This site is part portfolio, part field manual, and part build log. It documents the things I have built, broken, fixed, automated, and learned from.

docs.title: Alerting
docs.text: This page documents alerting ideas and notification patterns.

docs.title: Alert Types
docs.text: Alert Purpose Public exposure Detect unexpected reachable services Container status Know when services stop or restart Server health Track system issues Security events Surface items worth review Deal alerts Notify when criteria are met Workflow failures Know when automation breaks

docs.title: Alert Quality Rules
docs.text:
• Make the alert easy to read.
  • Include the thing that changed.
  • Include the action needed.
  • Avoid noisy repeated messages.
  • Use separate channels for separate alert types.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: A local audio processing lab for separating tracks and experimenting with music practice tools.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Musicians often need practice tracks, isolated parts, and flexible audio tools. Running these tools locally gives more control and avoids relying entirely on web services.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text:
The lab explores local audio separation and practice workflows:

  • Upload a track
  • Separate stems
  • Process locally
  • Use output for practice
  • Improve musician workflow

docs.title: Tools Used
docs.text:
• Python
  • Flask / FastAPI concepts
  • Audio separation tools
  • Docker
  • Unraid
  • GPU-assisted processing concepts

docs.title: Screenshots
docs.text:
Save screenshots here later:

docs/assets/images/projects/audio-lab/

Example Markdown once screenshots are added:

![Audio separation interface](../assets/images/projects/audio-lab/interface.png)

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: This project demonstrates local AI/audio tooling, self-hosting, and practical workflow design for music practice.

docs.title: Lessons Learned
docs.text:
• Local processing gives control but requires more setup.
  • Good UI matters when a tool is used repeatedly.
  • Creative projects still benefit from clean engineering notes.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: A lightweight incident response tracker designed for SOC-style workflows.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Incident response work can become scattered across chats, spreadsheets, tickets, and memory. Smaller teams need a simple way to track incidents, actions, status, ownership, notes, and follow-up tasks without overbuilding the process.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text:
The goal is to keep the workflow simple:

  • Open an incident
  • Assign ownership
  • Track status
  • Capture actions taken
  • Document artifacts and notes
  • Close with lessons learned

docs.title: Tools Used
docs.text:
• Web application prototype
  • Docker / self-hosted deployment
  • Unraid lab environment
  • Incident response workflow design
  • Future automation hooks

docs.title: Screenshots
docs.text:
Save screenshots here later:

docs/assets/images/projects/ir-tracker/

Example Markdown once screenshots are added:

![Incident dashboard](../assets/images/projects/ir-tracker/dashboard.png)

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: The project creates a practical way to demonstrate incident response process thinking, lightweight tooling, and technician-friendly workflow design.

docs.title: Lessons Learned
docs.text:
• Keep the workflow simple enough that a technician would actually use it.
  • Do not overbuild dashboards before the core incident process works.
  • A useful MVP is better than a complicated tool nobody wants to maintain.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: A workflow automation system that uses n8n to collect useful data and send clean notifications to Discord.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: A lot of home lab and personal ops work involves checking the same things repeatedly: server status, deal alerts, newly added media, exposure checks, and workflow results. Manual checking wastes time.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text:
Use n8n as the workflow engine and Discord as the notification layer.

Examples:

  • Scheduled checks
  • API pulls
  • Filtering and scoring
  • Normalized output
  • Discord channel alerts
  • Separate channels for different alert types

docs.title: Tools Used
docs.text:
• n8n
  • Discord webhooks
  • JavaScript function nodes
  • Scheduled triggers
  • Docker / Unraid
  • API integrations

docs.title: Screenshots
docs.text:
Save screenshots here later:

docs/assets/images/projects/n8n-discord/

Example Markdown once screenshots are added:

![n8n workflow](../assets/images/projects/n8n-discord/workflow.png)

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: This project shows practical automation skills: turning repeated checks into reliable workflows with readable outputs.

docs.title: Lessons Learned
docs.text:
• Good alerts need filtering.
  • Separate channels keep noise under control.
  • Normalizing messy data is usually the hardest part.
  • A workflow is only useful if it reduces human checking.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: A lightweight external exposure check that helps identify whether public-facing services are unexpectedly reachable.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Self-hosted labs often grow over time. Subdomains, proxy hosts, ports, DNS records, and exposed services can become hard to track. A simple recurring check helps catch surprises.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text: The workflow checks selected public endpoints and reports whether they appear reachable, blocked, redirected, or unexpected.

docs.title: Tools Used
docs.text:
• n8n
  • HTTP request nodes
  • Discord alerts
  • Cloudflare DNS / proxy concepts
  • Reverse proxy awareness
  • Basic exposure review process

docs.text:
• DNS, proxy, and firewall rules need periodic review.

  • Public services should be intentional, documented, and monitored.
